takeaway: A robot never knows exactly where it is: it keeps a best guess and a cloud of doubt, and moving grows the doubt while every measurement shrinks it.

selfCheck.question: Why can't it simply trust the GPS?
selfCheck.answer: GPS only accurate to about 4.9 m in open sky, worse near buildings and trees; one more imperfect reading; blend it with wheel counting and landmarks.

sentence: A robot can't be sure where it is. When it moves by counting wheel turns, small errors add up and its "cloud of doubt" grows. When it sees a landmark it already knows, the cloud shrinks. It keeps blending its own guess with these readings, trusting whichever is less doubtful, and that method is called a Kalman filter.
unclearTerms: "Where the landmark says it is" (a sign can't speak)
black ball on a stick (what it marks)
"trusting whichever has less doubt" (reading's doubt never drawn)

uncountedTerms.why: the concept the last step introduces

reason: My TAKEAWAY covers the same ideas: the robot is never sure where it is, it keeps a guess and a cloud of doubt, moving grows the cloud and looking at a landmark shrinks it; I only said "landmark" where the authors say "every measurement".
